name: Serverless functions
summary: Upload a function; the cloud runs it only when something happens.
howItWorks: You write a handler and choose what triggers it: an HTTP request, a new file, a queue message, a schedule. The platform starts instances on demand, runs as many in parallel as traffic needs, and shuts them down when idle. You pay per invocation and per millisecond of runtime, and there are no servers for you to patch.
analogy: A taxi instead of a car you own. It shows up when you call, you pay for the ride, and insurance and parking are someone else’s problem.
useWhen: Event-driven glue: resize an image on upload, react to a queue message
Spiky or low traffic, where idle servers would waste money
avoidWhen: Work that runs longer than the limit (15 minutes on AWS Lambda)
Latency-critical paths that can’t absorb an occasional cold start
Steady high throughput, where an always-on container is usually cheaper
example: Every time a sensor gateway uploads a compressed batch, a function unpacks it and writes the readings to the database. At night there are no uploads, so nothing runs and nothing is billed.

diagram.caption: Bursts of requests spin up new instances; amber marks a cold start. When traffic stops, idle instances time out one by one until none are left.

story: Cloud platforms had been hiding servers for a while before anyone called it serverless. Google App Engine’s 2008 preview ran web apps without machines to manage, in exchange for strict rules such as code written only in Python and responses due within a few seconds. In October 2012 Ken Fromm wrote in ReadWrite that cloud apps were “moving into a serverless world”. The word didn’t mean servers would vanish: “It simply means that developers no longer have to think that much about them.”

AWS Lambda, announced in November 2014, turned that into a concrete model. You uploaded a single function, said which event should run it (a file landing in S3, a change in DynamoDB, a record in Kinesis) and paid per request plus each 100 milliseconds of compute. Microsoft announced Azure Functions on March 31, 2016, Google’s Cloud Functions reached general availability in 2018, and Cloudflare Workers (2017) ran functions at the network edge in lightweight V8 isolates. In 2019 a Berkeley paper predicted that serverless “will grow to dominate the future of cloud computing”.
The model has since stretched: Cloud Run applied it to whole containers in 2019, and AWS’s durable functions (2025) let a function pause and resume across long workflows.

choices.choice: Code runs in response to events
choices.why: Instead of a server waiting for work, the platform starts your code when something happens. That turned cloud services into building blocks you could glue together with small functions.

choices.choice: Pay per invocation and per slice of runtime
choices.why: Billing in fractions of a second means idle code costs nothing and capacity scales to zero. The trade-off is the cold start when a new instance has to be created.
Early platforms capped requests at a minute and kept no local state, so they could start, stop and move instances freely. State lives in databases and queues instead.
Running strangers’ code in thousands of tiny instances needs isolation that starts in milliseconds, which is why platforms built V8 isolates (Cloudflare) and microVMs (AWS Firecracker).
